executive_summary: Five years of hourly PM2.5 in Beijing (41,757 valid hours) average 99 µg/m³ - 1.3× the national 24-hour limit and 7× the WHO guideline. The distribution is strongly right-skewed (skewness 1.80, median 72), so robust statistics and a log transform matter throughout. Pollution is driven by meteorology: calm air and south-easterly winds trap particles (mean 126 and 111 µg/m³) while north-westerly winds flush them out (70 µg/m³). Weather alone explains about 26% of hourly variance in a linear model; the best daily forecast (walk-forward ARIMA) cuts RMSE from 127 (naive) to 59 µg/m³.

findings.title: Heavily skewed, fat-tailed target
findings.detail: Mean 98.6 vs median 72.0; skewness 1.80, excess kurtosis 4.8. 4.25% of hours sit above the IQR upper fence. log(1+PM2.5) brings skewness close to zero.

findings.title: Winter and autumn are worst, by season and by hour
findings.detail: Season means: Winter 113, Spring 87, Summer 90, Autumn 104 µg/m³. Night hours are consistently higher than afternoon hours.

findings.title: Wind speed is the strongest single linear predictor
findings.detail: Pearson r(PM2.5, Iws) = -0.248; dew point r = 0.171. Spearman is larger in magnitude than Pearson for wind speed, pointing to a non-linear (saturating) relationship.

findings.title: Normality is rejected everywhere, CLT still works
findings.detail: Jarque-Bera on PM2.5: p 0. Yet the mean of n=30 random hours has skewness 0.33 and its spread matches σ/√n (16.7 vs 16.8).

findings.title: Season explains a significant share of daily variation
findings.detail: One-way ANOVA F(3, 1822) = 11.2, p = 2.8e-07, η² = 0.018. Tukey HSD separates winter/autumn from summer; Kruskal-Wallis agrees.

findings.title: No weekend effect; no 2010→2014 improvement
findings.detail: Weekend vs weekday Welch t = 0.91, p = 0.365. Paired t-test on 12 calendar months 2014 vs 2010: mean change -5.2 µg/m³, p = 0.632.

findings.title: Weather explains a modest share of hourly PM2.5
findings.detail: Model B (weather + wind direction): R² = 0.261, adjusted R² = 0.260, F = 1635 (p < 0.0001). Dew point has the largest standardised coefficient; adding wind dummies improves fit significantly (nested F p = 6.5e-294). The log-target model has better residual behaviour (Jarque-Bera skew -0.18 vs 1.75).

findings.title: Residuals are autocorrelated and heteroscedastic
findings.detail: Durbin-Watson = 0.13 (strong positive autocorrelation - hourly rows are not independent); Breusch-Pagan p = 0. OLS standard errors are therefore optimistic; a time-series model is needed.

findings.title: Random hold-out flatters time-ordered data
findings.detail: Random 80/20 test R² for the random forest is 0.432, but the chronological split (train 2010-13, test 2014) gives 0.303. 5-fold CV R² for linear regression: 0.260 ± 0.0053.

findings.title: Multivariate methods find the January 2013 episode
findings.detail: Mahalanobis flags 97 days, LOF 46, z-score 35. The top-ranked day is 2010-12-31 (daily mean 19 µg/m³, hourly max 28).

findings.title: SMOTE trades precision for recall on severe days
findings.detail: Severe days (> 200 µg/m³) are 9.53% of days (1:9). Logistic regression recall rises from 19% to 83% with SMOTE while precision falls from 54% to 41%. ROC-AUC barely moves (0.936 → 0.941) - resampling shifts the threshold, not the ranking.

findings.title: Level is stationary; seasonality is annual
findings.detail: ADF on monthly PM2.5: p = 0.000; first difference p = 1.2e-06. Linear trend -1.04 µg/m³ per year (p = 0.67) - no significant long-run trend 2010-2014. Seasonal strength 0.52.

findings.title: Short-horizon ARIMA beats naive; monthly forecasting is hard
findings.detail: Daily (61-day test): best model ARIMAX(1,0,1) + weather RMSE 59.0, MASE 0.80 vs naive RMSE 127.4. Monthly (12-month test): best Holt-Winters RMSE 26.7, MAPE 22%.

limitations: One monitoring station (US Embassy) and one weather station: results describe central Beijing, not the whole city.
2,067 hours (4.72%) have no PM2.5 reading and were dropped; 37 whole days were interpolated for the daily series.

Hourly observations are strongly autocorrelated (Durbin-Watson far below 2), so classical p-values from OLS, t-tests and ANOVA on hourly rows are too small. Daily aggregates were used for the tests where this matters.
No emission data (traffic, heating, industry) - weather can only explain the dispersion side of pollution, hence the modest R².
Forecast models are evaluated on a single chronological split (2014). A different test year would give different error numbers.
The ARIMAX model assumes the weather of the forecast day is known exactly; in practice it would come from a weather forecast with its own error.
SMOTE creates synthetic minority rows by interpolating between neighbours; with only ~140 severe days in training the synthetic points may not reflect real severe-day weather.
recommendations: Report PM2.5 with median and IQR, not mean and SD - the mean is pulled up by a few extreme days.
Issue public health warnings when the forecast shows calm or south-easterly wind with high dew point in winter; these three conditions carry most of the signal.
Use recall-oriented classifiers (SMOTE or class weights) for severe-day alerts: a missed hazardous day costs more than a false alarm.
Prefer walk-forward evaluation and chronological splits for any model that will be used operationally.
Add exogenous drivers (emissions, regional transport, boundary-layer height) to lift the explained variance beyond what local weather provides.
For monthly planning use seasonal-naive or Holt-Winters as a floor; the annual cycle is the only reliable monthly structure.
